children: Nvidia is already the dominant artificial-intelligence chip company. But its reach could extend even further next year, if CEO Jensen Huang is to be believed.
Speaking while on a trip to the U.K. on Thursday, Huang made a striking forecast-that he expects Nvidia to sell "twice as many chips next year as we do this year."

That was surprising. First, Nvidia doesn't generally give out forecasts about individual chip shipments. Second, it's a big number for a company that is already doing hundreds of billions in annual sales and has said it is constrained by supply-chain issues.

Huang was talking about chip volumes rather than overall revenue. Nvidia is already forecast to achieve 70% sales growth for its next fiscal year, which will end in January 2028, making it largely the same as the calendar year.

So chip volumes could double, but sales are expected to rise around 70%. Nvidia didn't respond to a Barron's request for comment to clarify what chips are included in the "twice as many" forecast, but Huang did say the driver was AI. That suggests the engine of growth will be the company's AI-related graphics-processing units (GPUs), central-processing units (CPUs) and networking chips rather than its video-gaming hardware.

While Nvidia doesn't disclose individual chip numbers, analysis firm Epoch AI estimates it sold around 4.46 million AI GPUs in 2025 and had sold about 3.39 million this year through the end of August. Assuming its monthly rate of sales stayed the same-a big assumption as Nvidia is ramping up production of its next-generation Vera Rubin hardware-that would put it on track to sell about 5.09 million AI GPUs this year.

That's not a rate of growth that would imply doubling volumes next year, but there are a few things to consider. Increasingly, Nvidia sells its AI chips via its NV72 server racks, which package together 72 GPUs as well as 36 CPUs and a number of networking chips. Huang might be including the total number of chips across the server rack in his estimate.
The numbers add up quickly when you count all the chips within a server and assume racks will account for a greater share of future sales.

Max Weinbach, an analyst at market-research firm Creative Strategies, estimated earlier this year that Nvidia was set to ship between 70,000 and 80,000 of its Grace Blackwell server racks this year. Assuming all of them were NV72 configurations, the midpoint would indicate 5.4 million AI GPUs, 2.7 million CPUs, and millions of networking chips.

So what about 2027? Research firm TrendForce estimates that shipments of NVL72 racks will grow by more than 50% in 2027 from this year. That could account for a substantial part of Huang's doubling forecast and imply huge revenue growth, since Vera Rubin hardware will come at higher average prices than Blackwell racks.

However, volume growth outstripping revenue growth indicates Nvidia also expects to sell a lot of lower-priced chips. One candidate is stand-alone CPUs, which the company launched this year and said it expects to become a multibillion-dollar business.
Other possible products to account for the remaining volumes include AI chips for the Chinese market, stand-alone networking chips, and the company's new PC chip, which it unveiled earlier this year.
Nvidia might not like talking too much about individual chip sales anymore, but it's still worth shareholders having an idea of how the world's largest company intends to keep growing.
Nvidia shares were down 0.2% in early trading Friday.
